summary: Defines FLUTE, File Delivery over Unidirectional Transport, a protocol for sending files one way over the Internet, especially suited to multicast networks. It builds on Asynchronous Layered Coding, the base protocol for massively scalable multicast distribution. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: FLUTE sends files over a one-way network, such as a multicast group, where receivers cannot send anything back. It works by putting a description of each file into the same stream of packets as the file itself, so a receiver can tell what it has received and can put it together.

questions: how to deliver files over multicast
how does flute deliver files over multicast
what is a file delivery table
subtitle: How to broadcast files to many receivers at once, with no feedback channel, by sending a table that describes each file.

tldr.problem: Sending a file to thousands of machines over IP multicast is awkward: the network offers no way to ask who received what, and the receivers need to know what the bytes they are receiving actually mean.
tldr.mechanism: FLUTE defines a file delivery session on top of Asynchronous Layered Coding. Each file is given a number, and a File Delivery Table travels in the same stream as the files, describing the name, type, size and encoding of each one, so a receiver can assemble what it receives.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6726 is a Proposed Standard from November 2012 that obsoletes the experimental RFC 3926 and is not backwards compatible with it. The FLUTE version number was raised from 1 to 2 because the LCT building block changed in the meantime.

today: RFC 6726 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2012. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 3926, and it is not backwards compatible with that version because the LCT building block it sits on changed in the meantime. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction and Applicability
sections.content:
This document defines FLUTE version 2, a protocol for the unidirectional delivery of files over the Internet. The specification is not backwards compatible with the previous experimental version of RFC 3926. It builds on Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) version 1, RFC 5775, the base protocol designed for massively scalable multicast distribution, and on the Layered Coding Transport building block, RFC 5651. ALC defines transport of arbitrary binary objects. For file delivery, mere transport of objects is not enough: the end systems need to know what the objects actually represent. FLUTE is the mechanism for signalling and mapping the properties of files to concepts of ALC in a way that allows receivers to assign those parameters for received objects. Throughout the document, the term file relates to an object as discussed in ALC.

Although the specification frequently uses multicast addressing as an example, the techniques are similarly applicable with unicast addressing. The document adds four things to ALC: the definition of a file delivery session built on top of ALC, including transport details and timing constraints; in-band signalling of the transport parameters of the ALC session; in-band signalling of the properties of delivered files; and details associated with the multiplexing of multiple files within a session.

The intended application space is the delivery of large and small files to many hosts, using delivery sessions of several seconds or more, for instance large software updates delivered to many hosts simultaneously, or continuous but segmented data such as time-lined text for subtitling. It is also suitable for the basic transport of metadata such as Session Description Protocol files. Massive scalability is a primary design goal. IP multicast is inherently massively scalable, but the best-effort service it provides has no session management, congestion control or reliability, and FLUTE provides all of this by using ALC and IP multicast without sacrificing the inherent scalability of IP multicast.

FLUTE requires connectivity between a sender and receivers but does not require connectivity from receivers to a sender, so it works with most types of networks, including LANs, WANs, Intranets, the Internet, asymmetric networks, wireless networks and satellite networks. It is compatible with both IPv4 and IPv6, and works with both multicast models, Any-Source Multicast and Source-Specific Multicast.

The RFC names the weaknesses too. FLUTE congestion control depends on the ability of a receiver to change multicast subscriptions between groups supporting different rates or layered codings, which not every network allows. FLUTE provides reliability using the FEC building block, but it does not provide a way for senders to verify that receivers got the files, and that method is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is built for sending the same thing to a very large number of machines at once, where the receivers cannot phone home. It adds error correction so that a receiver can recover a file even if some packets are lost, and it needs the network to offer some way of slowing the sender down when the link is busy.

sections.title: The File Delivery Session
sections.content:
An ALC/LCT session consists of a set of logically grouped ALC/LCT channels associated with a single sender sending ALC/LCT packets for one or more objects. An ALC/LCT channel is defined by the combination of a sender and an address associated with the channel by the sender. A receiver joins a channel to start receiving the data packets sent to the channel, and leaves it to stop.

One of the fields carried in the ALC/LCT header is the Transport Session Identifier (TSI), an integer carried in a field of size 16, 32 or 48 bits, although the TSI may be carried by other means, in which case it is absent from the LCT header. The pair of source IP address and TSI uniquely identifies a session. The TSI is scoped by the IP address, so the same TSI may be used by several source addresses at once, and the receiver uses the pair from each packet to identify the session. When a session carries multiple objects, the Transmission Object Identifier (TOI) field within the ALC/LCT header names the object used to generate each packet, and each object is associated with a unique TOI within the scope of a session.

A FLUTE session consistent with this specification MUST use FLUTE version 2, carried within the EXT_FDT header extension, and MUST use ALC version 1 and LCT version 1. If multiple FLUTE sessions are sent to a channel, receivers MUST determine the protocol version from the version fields and the address and TSI pair. A new receiver might not know the version at first, because not every LCT packet carries the EXT_FDT header; it MAY keep an open binding between the TSI and the version until the header arrives.

When FLUTE is used for file delivery, the ALC/LCT session is called a file delivery session, and the ALC/LCT concept of object denotes either a file or a File Delivery Table Instance. Three rules follow. The TOI field MUST be included in ALC packets sent within a FLUTE session, except that packets with the Close Session flag set to 1 and no payload SHALL NOT carry the TOI. The TOI value 0 is reserved for the delivery of File Delivery Table Instances, and each non-expired FDT Instance is uniquely identified by an FDT Instance ID within the EXT_FDT header. Each file in a file delivery session MUST be associated with a TOI greater than 0 in the scope of that session. Information carried in the headers and payload of a packet is scoped by the source IP address and the TSI, and information particular to the object is further scoped by the TOI for files, and by both the TOI and the FDT Instance ID for FDT Instance objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is one sender sending to one address. Each file in it gets a number, and the number zero is reserved for the table that describes the files. The receiver tells sessions apart by the sender's address together with a session number.

sections.title: The File Delivery Table
sections.content:
The File Delivery Table provides a means to describe the attributes associated with files delivered in the session. Attributes related to the delivery of a file are the TOI value that represents the file, the FEC Object Transmission Information including the FEC Encoding ID and, if relevant, the FEC Instance ID, the size of the transmission object carrying the file, and the aggregate rate of sending packets to all channels. Attributes related to the file itself are its name, identification and location, specified by the URI, its media type, its size, its encoding and its message digest. Some of these attributes MUST be included in the file description entry for a file, and others are optional.

Logically, the FDT is a set of file description entries for files to be delivered in the session. Each file description entry MUST include the TOI for the file it describes and the URI identifying the file, and the TOI is how FLUTE names the ALC/LCT data packets used for delivery of the file. Each entry may also contain one or more descriptors that map the attributes above to the file.

Each file delivery session MUST have an FDT local to that session, and the FDT MUST provide a file description entry mapped to a TOI for each file appearing within the session. An object delivered in the session but not described in the FDT, other than the FDT itself, is not considered a file belonging to the session, and an object received with an unmapped TOI SHOULD in general be ignored by a FLUTE receiver. A client that joins an active session MAY receive data packets for a TOI greater than zero before receiving any FDT Instance, and system performance might be improved by caching such packets within a reasonable time window and storage size, though such optimizations are implementation specific.

Within the session, the FDT is delivered as FDT Instances. An FDT Instance contains one or more file description entries of the FDT, and any instance can be equal to, a subset of, a superset of, overlapping with or complementary to any other. A given instance may be repeated several times during a session, even after instances with higher FDT Instance ID numbers have been transmitted. A receiver keeps an FDT database of the file description entries it has received, and at any time the contents of that database represent the receiver's current view of the FDT. Since each receiver behaves independently, it SHOULD NOT be assumed that the contents of the database are the same for all receivers of a session.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a list, one entry per file, giving each file a number and describing it: where it came from, what type it is, how big it is, how it was compressed and how to check it. The receiver keeps its own copy of the list and updates it as more arrives.

sections.title: Dynamics of FDT Instances
sections.content:
A set of rules defines how FDT Instances behave within a session. For every file delivered, there MUST be a file description entry included in at least one FDT Instance sent within the session, containing at a minimum the mapping between the TOI and the URI. An FDT Instance MAY appear in any part of the session, and its packets MAY be interleaved with packets for other files or other instances. The TOI value 0 MUST be reserved for FDT Instances. The FDT Instance is identified by a new fixed-length LCT header extension, EXT_FDT, and any ALC/LCT packet carrying an FDT Instance MUST include it.

It is RECOMMENDED that an FDT Instance containing the description of a file be sent at least once before the file itself is sent, so that receivers do not receive file data ahead of the description of it, which would have to be buffered or discarded. That possibility cannot be completely eliminated, since the first transmission of FDT data might be lost. Within a session, any TOI greater than zero MAY be described more than once, but subsequent instances MUST NOT change the parameters already described for a specific TOI.

An FDT Instance is valid until its expiration time, expressed in the instance payload as a UTF-8 decimal representation of a 32-bit unsigned integer, which represents the 32 most significant bits of a 64-bit NTP time value, giving the time in seconds relative to 0 hours 1 January 1900 in the prime epoch. Handling the time wraparound, which happens in 2036, requires the associated epoch to be considered, and both a sender and a receiver determine which 136-year epoch the expiration time belongs to by choosing the epoch for which it is closest to the current time. The RFC works through an example: a session started on February 7th 2036 at NTP time 4,294,944,000, with an expiry time of 149,504, gives an instance that expires exactly on February 9th 2036.

The space of FDT Instance IDs is limited by the 20-bit field in the EXT_FDT header, so senders must keep a large enough supply available when specifying expiration times. The receiver MUST NOT use a received FDT Instance to interpret packets received beyond its expiration time, and a sender MUST use an expiration time in the future relative to its Sender Current Time.

Any FEC Encoding ID MAY be used for sending FDT Instances, with the default being the Compact No-Code FEC Encoding ID 0, which implies that the Source Block Number and Encoding Symbol ID lengths both default to 16 bits each. If the receiver does not support the FEC scheme indicated by the FEC Encoding ID, it MUST NOT decode the associated FDT. It is RECOMMENDED that the mechanisms used for file attribute delivery achieve a delivery probability higher than the file recovery probability, and that the file attributes be delivered at this higher priority before the delivery of the associated files begins, since a receiver generally needs an FDT Instance describing a file before it can recover the file itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The description of a file should arrive before the file itself, so the receiver knows what to do with the bytes. Each instance of the table has an expiry time, written as a time value with a 136-year era, and the receiver must stop using an instance once it has expired.

sections.title: Structure of FDT Instance Packets
sections.content:
FDT Instances are carried in ALC packets with TOI equal to 0 and with an additional REQUIRED LCT header extension, the FDT Instance Header. That header, EXT_FDT, contains the FDT Instance ID that uniquely identifies FDT Instances within a file delivery session, and its placement is the same as that of any other LCT header extension. The FDT Instance is encoded for transmission, like any other object, using an FEC scheme, which may be the Compact No-Code scheme. The LCT header extensions are followed by the FEC Payload ID, and finally the encoding symbols for the FDT Instance, which contain one or more file description entries. An FDT Instance MAY span several ALC packets, and the FDT Instance Header is carried in each of them and is identical for all of them. All integer fields are carried in big-endian or network order, and all ALC/LCT packets are sent using UDP.

The EXT_FDT header extension is a new fixed-length, ALC-specific LCT header extension with a Header Extension Type of 192. It carries the version of FLUTE in a 4-bit field, which MUST be set to 2 in any ALC packet that carries an FDT Instance and belongs to a session as specified here, and the FDT Instance ID in a 20-bit field. For each session, the numbering of FDT Instances starts from 0 and is incremented by one for each subsequent instance. After reaching the maximum value of 2^20-1, the numbering starts from the smallest FDT Instance ID value assigned to an expired instance, and when wraparound occurs the smaller value is considered logically higher than the greater one, so the values always increase logically. Senders MUST NOT reuse an FDT Instance ID value that is in use for a non-expired instance, and receipt of an instance that reuses such a value MUST be considered an error case. Receivers MUST be ready to handle wraparound and missing instance IDs that result in increments larger than one.

The FDT Instance itself is an XML structure with a single root element FDT-Instance. That element MUST contain the Expires attribute, giving the expiration time, and MAY contain the Complete attribute, a boolean. When Complete is true, it signals that this instance includes the set of File entries that exhausts both the files delivered so far and the files to be delivered in the session, so no new data will be provided in future instances. When all instances received so far have no Complete attribute, the receiver MUST consider the session incomplete. The FDT-Instance element MAY also contain attributes giving common parameters for all files of an instance, and where the same attribute appears in both the FDT-Instance and a File element, the value in the File element takes precedence.

Each file declared in an instance has a single file description entry, represented by a File element that is a child of the FDT-Instance structure. Each File element MUST contain at least two attributes: TOI, which MUST be assigned a valid TOI value, and Content-Location, which MUST be assigned a syntactically valid URI identifying the file to be delivered, for example one with the http or file scheme. Only one Content-Location attribute is allowed for each file, and it MUST be considered a string that identifies a file. If two File elements declare the same Content-Location but different TOI values, the element in the instance with the greater FDT Instance ID is considered to declare a newer instance of the same file. Other attributes may be present: Content-Type SHOULD be included, Content-Length MUST be used where a length is described, Content-Encoding MUST be included whenever content encoding is applied, and Content-MD5 MUST be used where the MD5 message digest is described. The MD5 attribute provides a decoded object integrity service, and it MUST NOT be regarded as a security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is an XML document, and each file is one element in it. It travels in ordinary packets, with a small extra header holding the version and the number of the table instance. The receiver can tell which instance a packet belongs to from that header.

sections.title: Channels, Congestion Control and Timing
sections.content:
ALC/LCT has a concept of channels and congestion control, and the RFC describes four scenarios in which FLUTE is envisioned to be applied: a single channel with a single-rate congestion control protocol; multiple channels with a multiple-rate congestion control protocol, in which case the FDT Instances MAY be delivered on more than one channel; a single channel without congestion control supplied by ALC, but only when in a controlled network environment where flow and congestion control is provided by other means; and multiple channels without congestion control supplied by ALC, again only in a controlled environment, in which case the FDT Instances MAY be delivered on more than one channel.

With one channel, the notion of prior and after is intuitively defined for the delivery of objects with respect to their delivery times. With multiple channels it is not straightforward: an object may begin to be delivered on one or more channels before the delivery of a second object begins, and the use of multiple layers may mean that the second object is completed before the first. This is not a problem when objects are delivered sequentially using a single channel, so if an application has a mandatory or critical requirement that the first transmission object must complete before the second one, it is RECOMMENDED that only a single channel be used.

Furthermore, if multiple channels are used, a receiver joined at a low reception rate will only be joined to the lower layers of the session. Since receiving FDT Instances has a higher priority than receiving files, because recovering a file depends on having its description, the RFC makes two recommendations. The layers to which packets for FDT Instances are sent SHOULD NOT be biased towards those layers that lower-rate receivers have not joined: it is fine to put all the packets for an instance into the lowest layer, if that layer carries enough packets to deliver the table to higher-rate receivers in a reasonable time, but not fine to put all of them into higher layers that only higher-rate receivers receive. And if FDT Instances are generally longer than one encoding symbol and some packets for them are sent to layers that lower-rate receivers do not receive, an FEC encoding other than Compact No-Code FEC Encoding ID 0 SHOULD be used to deliver them, because in that case a lower-rate receiver will not receive all the packets sent for the instance even when there is no packet loss in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: A session can run on one channel or on several layers of different speeds. The table must be sent where slow receivers can get it, because a file cannot be assembled without it. If the table is spread over several packets, those packets need error correction of their own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A content delivery system is potentially subject to attacks, which may target the network, for example by creating congestion; the Content Delivery Protocol, for example by compromising the normal behaviour of FLUTE; or the content itself, for example by corrupting the files being transmitted. These attacks can be launched against the data flow itself, such as by sending forged packets; against the session control parameters, such as by corrupting the session description, the FDT Instances or the ALC/LCT control parameters, whether sent in-band or out-of-band; or against some associated building blocks, such as the congestion control component.

Against the data flow, the types of attack are those meant to give access to a confidential file and those that try to corrupt the file being transmitted, for example by injecting malicious code or by preventing a receiver from using the file. Access control to the file is typically provided by encryption, which can be done over the whole file before applying FEC protection, or on a packet-by-packet basis when IPsec and ESP are used. If confidentiality is a concern, the RFC recommends using one of these.

The RFC then introduces a mandatory-to-implement, but not necessarily to-use, security configuration. Since FLUTE relies on ALC/LCT, it inherits the baseline secure ALC operation of RFC 5775. Security is achieved by means of IPsec with ESP in transport mode, which can provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, content integrity, anti-replay and limited traffic flow confidentiality. RFC 5775 specifies that data origin authentication, content integrity and anti-replay services SHALL be supported, and that the confidentiality service is RECOMMENDED. If a short-lived session may rely on manual keying, an automated key management scheme is also RECOMMENDED, especially for long-lived sessions.

The recommended solution for FLUTE therefore provides per-packet security, with data origin authentication, integrity verification and anti-replay. This is sufficient to prevent most of the in-band attacks listed in the RFC. If confidentiality is required, per-packet encryption SHOULD also be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone on the network could inject packets or alter the table, so the RFC calls for each packet to be authenticated and protected against replay, using IPsec. Encryption of the file itself is a separate question, and is recommended when the content must stay private.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3926
sections.content:
The FLUTE protocol version was incremented from 1 to 2 because of concerns about backwards compatibility. The LCT header changed between RFC 3451 and RFC 5651: in RFC 3451 the T and R fields of the LCT header indicate the presence of Sender Current Time and Expected Residual Time, whereas in RFC 5651 these fields MUST be set to zero and MUST be ignored by receivers, with the EXT_TIME header extensions able to convey the information if needed. RFC 5651 is therefore not backwards compatible with RFC 3451, even though both use LCT version 1. FLUTE version 1 as specified in RFC 3926 MUST use RFC 3451, while FLUTE version 2 as specified here MUST use RFC 5651, so an implementation that relies on RFC 3926 and RFC 3451 will not be backwards compatible with FLUTE as specified in this document.

Other changes listed by the RFC include updating dependencies on other RFCs to revised versions, for example changing the ALC reference from RFC 3450 to RFC 5775 and the LCT reference from RFC 3451 to RFC 5651; adding a clarification of the use of FLUTE for unicast communications in Section 1.1.4; clarifying how to deliver the FDT reliably and the possibility of out-of-band delivery of FDT information; clarifying how to address FDT Instance expiration time wraparound with the notion of the NTPv4 epoch; clarifying what should be considered erroneous situations in the definition of the FDT Instance ID, in particular that a receiver must be ready to handle wraparounds and missing FDT Instances; updating Section 7.5 to define IPsec with ESP as a mandatory-to-implement security solution; removing the Statement of Intent from Section 1, which was meant to clarify the experimental status of RFC 3926 and does not apply here; adding a clarification of XML-DSIG near the end of Section 3; replacing the phrase complete FDT with more descriptive text in Section 3.2; clarifying the figure showing the encoding symbols for an FDT Instance; adding semantics for the case where two TOIs refer to the same Content-Location, now in line with the way that 3GPP and Digital Video Broadcasting standards interpret that case; modifying the XML Schema of the FDT Instance on advice from various sources, for example supporting extension by element and changing the namespace definition to URN format; and clarifying the extensibility of the FDT schema.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version of this protocol was an experiment. The main reason it could not simply be updated in place is that the transport layer it sat on was itself replaced, so a receiver of the old format cannot read the new one.

viz.caption: AN EXAMPLE FDT INSTANCE, FROM APPENDIX B OF RFC 6726

data.title: FDT Instance example
data.code:
<FDT-Instance xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
  xsi:schemaLocation="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:fdt
                      ietf-flute-fdt.xsd"
  Expires="2890842807">
  <File
    Content-Location="http://www.example.com/menu/tracklist.html"
    TOI="1"
    Content-Type="text/html"/>
  <File
    Content-Location="http://www.example.com/tracks/track1.mp3"
    TOI="2"
    Content-Length="6100"
    Content-Type="audio/mp3"
    Content-Encoding="gzip"
    Content-MD5="+VP5IrWploFkZWc11iLDdA=="
    Some-Private-Extension-Tag="abc123"/>
</FDT-Instance>

viz.caption: THE STRUCTURE OF A FILE DELIVERY TABLE

root.label: FDT-Instance
root.note: XML root element, with an Expires attribute

viz.caption: THE ATTRIBUTES A FILE DESCRIPTION ENTRY CAN CARRY

items.title: TOI
items.text: The number that names this file in the session. Required.

items.title: Content-Location
items.text: A URI identifying the file. Required.

items.title: Content-Type
items.text: The media type of the file, such as text/html.

items.title: Content-Length
items.text: The length of the file in octets.

items.title: Transfer-Length
items.text: The length of the object as transported, when it differs from the file length.

items.title: Content-Encoding
items.text: The encoding applied before transport, such as gzip. Required when an encoding is applied.

items.title: Content-MD5
items.text: A digest of the file for checking that it arrived intact. Not a security mechanism.

items.title: FEC Object Transmission Information
items.text: How to recover the file with error correction, including the FEC Encoding ID and instance.
